references.text: Jesus demonstrated his supernatural knowledge when he said that he had seen Nathanael under the fig tree ([ref:Joh 1:48|John 1:48]). This is what Nathanael believes, and Jesus promises him even greater things.
Right after this promise to see "greater things," Jesus explains what this entails: heaven opened and God's angels ascending and descending over the Son of Man ([ref:Joh 1:51|John 1:51]).

The water miracle at Cana was the first of the "greater things" that Jesus promised his disciples they would see. Here he revealed his glory, and the disciples believed in him ([ref:Joh 2:11|John 2:11]).
Jesus says that the Father will show him "greater works than these, so that you may marvel" ([ref:Joh 5:20|John 5:20]), which connects to the promise that Nathanael would see greater things.

At Lazarus' tomb, Jesus said to Martha: "Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?" ([ref:Joh 11:40|John 11:40]). Faith comes before seeing the greater things, just as Jesus also told Nathanael.

Jesus promises that whoever believes in him will do the same works as he does, yes, even greater ones ([ref:Joh 14:12|John 14:12]). This connects to the promise of "greater things" in the conversation with Nathanael.

After the resurrection, Jesus said to Thomas: "Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe" ([ref:Joh 20:29|John 20:29]). The pattern of believing after seeing, and the promise of something greater, mirrors the conversation with Nathanael.

Jacob's dream of a ladder between heaven and earth with angels ascending and descending ([ref:1 Mos 28:12|Gen 28:12]) is the background for the "greater things" Jesus explains in the next verse ([ref:Joh 1:51|John 1:51]), where he applies the image to himself as the Son of Man.
